messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sofia, a 27-year-old HVAC technician, presented for therapy six months after an abduction and assault. The event occurred after a late-night service call, when she was forced into a vehicle and held for two days in a locked basement. Her primary tormentor was a woman, who repeatedly told Sofia she was weak and had made a fatal mistake by being in the wrong place at the wrong time. Sofia was eventually released, but the psychological wounds have refused to heal. She reports that the memory of the event feels alien, as if she is watching a film about someone else. When fragments do break through—the scent of stale air, the metallic click of a lock—she is flooded not with fear, but with a hot, paralyzing shame for what she perceives as her own failure to fight back. The emotional overwhelm is so intense that she has to physically shake her head and focus on a complex task, like calibrating a thermostat, just to push the images away.

In the months since, Sofia has come to believe she is permanently damaged. This conviction that she has changed for the worse fuels a pervasive sense of threat that dictates her daily life. The belief that you can never truly know who will harm you has transformed her world into a landscape of potential dangers. This means she now spends several minutes each night checking and re-checking the locks on her apartment door and windows, and wakes frequently, her body rigid, listening for any sound that might signal an intruder. This constant state of alert has reinforced her self-doubt; the fact that she is always jumpy, dropping a wrench if a client speaks unexpectedly, serves as daily proof that she can no longer trust herself to do the right thing, either at work or in keeping herself safe. Her profound sense of being broken also makes the memory of the assault feel more toxic and shameful, cementing the idea that she was somehow complicit in her own suffering.

The intrusive memories themselves have become a direct source of threat. A fleeting image of the basement door is enough to send her heart racing, compelling her to scan her surroundings for escape routes, even when sitting in her own work van. These memory fragments also prime her to be hyper-aware of specific triggers. After one particularly vivid flashback, she found herself staring at a female cashier, her mind racing, unable to shake the association between the woman’s presence and a feeling of imminent danger. This pervasive sense of threat, in turn, has amplified her negative appraisals of herself and the world. Every night she wakes in a panic is another piece of evidence that she is irreparably broken. The constant vigilance has also made her exquisitely sensitive to triggers, causing her to perceive threats where none exist; a coworker with a bandaged hand becomes a source of visceral unease, and the sight of any locked door feels like a personal warning.

This cycle has become most acute in her work as an HVAC technician. A routine call to a single woman’s apartment last week became an ordeal. Being alone with a woman immediately triggered a profound sense of entrapment and danger. Sofia’s breathing grew shallow, and she felt an overwhelming urge to flee, convinced that this client, like her attacker, could not be trusted. The feeling of having no options but to finish the job left her trembling. This experience, and others like it, has led her to start turning down service calls to single-occupant residences, a pattern her supervisor has begun to notice. She sought therapy after realizing her world was shrinking to the four walls of her apartment. She feels she is losing control, and her deepest fear is that the woman from the basement was right—that she is fundamentally weak and has been changed for the worse, forever.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe how Sofia's negative beliefs about herself or the world cause her to be more sensitive or hyper-aware of triggers.
